reader: AI reader 3 (appraisal re-reading, papers read in the app's browser)

domains.reason: The Abstract says only that the authors examine the current literature; there is no methods section, search strategy or selection criteria for the 64 references.

Studies are taken at face value: autopsy series are summarised as showing that methamphetamine clearly increases coronary artery disease, and apolipoprotein E knockout mouse studies are called direct evidence, with no discussion of confounding (tobacco, cocaine or other drug use are not mentioned); the only appraisal remark is that sudden-death studies suffer from retrospective adjudication bias.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.reason: Only 1 of 64 references (ref 44, Vozenilek et al.) includes an author of the review, and it supports a general point on atherosclerosis biology rather than a key finding.

Mechanistic proposals in the body are usually hedged (may, could, would be predicted to, mechanisms remain unknown), but the Summary restates associations and animal findings as established human effects (methamphetamine clearly induces cardiovascular dysfunction; induces mitochondrial dysfunction and myocyte death driving cardiomyopathy).

Little that cuts against the thesis is presented: the review notes minimal data for persistent hypertension and lower cholesterol and obesity in users, but cites no null or conflicting studies and does not consider alternative explanations for the associations.
The Background says only that the authors review some open questions and propose a model; there is no methods section, search strategy or selection criteria for the 108 references.

No study-level quality or risk-of-bias assessment; appraisal is limited to remarks on why prevalence estimates vary (populations, self-report vs diagnostic instruments) and on scarce evidence (one eligible trial in a Cochrane review, a cited dearth of validation research), while key figures such as the 25% conversion rate and the shared susceptibility genes are presented at face value.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.reason: Only 3 of 108 references (12, 41, 51; Mordal/Medhus/Bramness) are from the authors' group, and they support peripheral points (drug findings among acute admissions, symptoms of amphetamine-positive patients).

The stress-vulnerability model is explicitly labelled a hypothesis in its own section, but clinical implications (closer monitoring, discouraging further use, a rationale for preventive treatment) are drawn directly from the untested model, and some mechanistic and genetic statements are worded as established.

It reports evidence that cuts against a single-entity view (faster and more complete recovery from amphetamine psychosis, the claim that Japanese chronic amphetamine psychosis is a separate entity), counter-arguments in the parallel cannabis debate, and both sides of the antipsychotic-treatment question.

A short CMAJ 'Mechanisms and innovations' review with no methods section and no statement of how its 38 references were found or chosen; sources include Erowid, product monographs and a personal communication.

No formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment; evidence is graded only informally (labelled preliminary, very preliminary or needing confirmation), and some statements carry no citation (for example that dopamine-receptor blockers do not block methamphetamine liking).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.reason: Only 1 of 38 references is from the author's group (ref 20, Moszczynska et al. 2004, introduced as the author's own finding), but it is cited three times and is the sole human source for striatal dopamine depletion and the modest transporter decrease, with no imaging studies cited for that point.

Hypotheses are consistently flagged with hedges (mechanism not completely understood, probably, could involve, still debated), and treatment ideas such as deep brain stimulation or cognitive enhancers are presented as strategies that might be considered.

It reports findings against simple readings: no evidence of dopamine-terminal damage at therapeutic doses, uncertainty whether the transporter decrease reflects terminal loss, receptor blockers not blocking liking, and a negative sertraline trial.

Methods › Search strategy and study screening: one reviewer screened titles and abstracts and a second reviewed every record marked as excluded; full texts were screened by two independent reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by a third, so eligibility decisions were made in duplicate.

Methods › Data extraction: one reviewer extracted the data and a second checked them; quality-index data were extracted by one reviewer and double-checked by a second, with a third resolving discrepancies (also stated under Limitations as independent checking of screening and extraction). This is extraction with full verification, not two independent extractions, so a stricter reading could answer no.

domains.domain: Item 11: appropriate methods for statistical combination
domains.reason: Methods › Data analysis: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling of CMRs and SMRs, chosen because high heterogeneity was expected; I² was reported and heterogeneity explored by subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses (author-reported vs imputed SMRs; excluding the HIV-positive cohort). Caveat: pooled estimates rest on I² of about 97–98%.

domains.domain: Item 13: risk of bias accounted for in interpretation
domains.reason: Methods › Data extraction applies a nine-criterion quality index; quality variables (case ascertainment, completeness, representativeness) were entered in meta-regressions; Discussion › Limitations interprets the results in their light (quality variables not associated with mortality except sampling frame, where single-city samples had higher mortality; unclear cause-of-death ascertainment).
